rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dates the whole surah to Mecca, probably around the middle of the Meccan period.
rows.anchor: this surah was re vealed in its entirety in Mecca, most probably

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah centers on resurrection and the certainty that every person must answer to God for earthly deeds.
rows.anchor: deals mainly w ith the prospect of resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because people readily go astray, they continually need prophetic guidance, explaining the earlier-prophet narratives in verses 75–148.
rows.anchor: man is apt to err (cf. yerse 71

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's central message is God's oneness, beyond anything people can define about Him.
rows.anchor: your God is One

rows.speaker: earliest authorities
rows.claim: Almost all earliest authorities read azwaj as people alike in disposition, of the same kind or ilk.
rows.anchor: including 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, As-Suddi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to 4:1 and its note for the parallel discussion of the first human pair.
rows.anchor: See 4:1 and the corresponding note 1.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eight pairs are male and female animals from four kinds: sheep, goats, camels, and bovines.
rows.anchor: the male and the female of four kinds of cattle (sheep, goats, camels and bovine cattle)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the same cattle in 6:143–144, where they figure in baseless pre-Islamic taboos, here they are God's lawful gift.
rows.anchor: meaningless, superstitious taboos of pre-Islamic times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their mention reminds people that God supplies their sustenance and that they depend entirely on Him.
rows.anchor: God who provides his sustenance and that, therefore, man is utterly dependent on Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three darknesses denote the womb, the membrane around the embryo, and prenatal blindness; embryonic stages are repeatedly mentioned in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: the darkness of the womb, the membrane enveloping the embryo, and its pre-natal blindness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing question literally asks how people are turned away, meaning turned away from the truth.
rows.anchor: Lit., "how, then, are you turned away?" - i.e., from the truth.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari takes the particle wa to indicate temporal precedence, so the gates have been opened before the people arrive; compare 38:50.
rows.anchor: which in this case denotes precedence in time (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Classical commentators understand inheriting paradise metaphorically as the blessed receiving their rightful due or portion.
rows.anchor: According to all the classical commentators, the concept of "heritage" is used here metaphorically

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ard can mean something spread, especially in poetry, which leads Asad to render it here as 'expanse.'
rows.anchor: the connotation of "anything that is spread" (cf. Lane 1, 48)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-'arsh is a metaphor for God's absolute dominion, so Asad renders it as the throne of His almightiness.
rows.anchor: Whenever the term al-'arsh ("the throne [of God]") occurs in the Qur'an, tt is used as a metaphor for His absolute dominion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels surrounding the throne are also described metaphorically; Asad refers readers to his explanation at 40:7.
rows.anchor: The mention of the "angels surrounding" it has, obviously, a metaphorical meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final clause literally says, 'it will be said.'
rows.anchor: Lit., "it will be said"

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: For hawlaha, Zamakhshari explains the phrase as meaning near it, as in 27:8.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari's explanation of the expression hawlaha occurring in 27:8 in the sense of "near it"

rows.speaker: Baydawi
rows.claim: Baydawi reads the angels' carrying and surrounding the throne metaphorically as mindfulness and governance, or as a metonym for nearness, dignity, and service to God's will; Asad follows this interpretation.
rows.anchor: Baydawi states explicitly that the "bearing" of God's throne of almightiness (al-'arsh - see note 43 on 7:54) must be understood in a metaphorical sense

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Most classical commentators infer that only angels are near the throne from 39:75; Asad accepts angels are included but rejects their exclusivity.
rows.anchor: most of the classical commentators - obviously basing their view on the symbolic image

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because hamala can mean bearing responsibility, the verse also includes people conscious of God's almightiness who enact that awareness in their own and others' lives.
rows.anchor: it applies here not only to angels but also to all human beings who are conscious of the tremendous implications

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this context, ayah means 'parable,' as the sequence makes clear.
rows.anchor: in this instance the term ayah (lit., "sign" or "[divine] message") is used in the sense of "parable"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's title comes from zukhruf in verse 35.
rows.anchor: Deriving its title from the incidental mention of the word zukhruf in verse 35

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah argues that assigning divinity to anything besides God is spiritually destructive and logically inadmissible.
rows.anchor: spiritually destructive but also logically inadmissible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spiritual error usually comes from blindly following ancestral belief, a theme stated in verses 22–23.
rows.anchor: blind adherence to what they regard as the faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's claim that the waters were beneath him means they were at his command, referring to the Nile irrigation network controlled by royal power.
rows.anchor: a reference to the imposing irrigation system originating in the Nile and controlled by royal power

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the command to honor parents with the references to doers of good in 46:12–14 and parallels at 29:8 and 31:14.
rows.anchor: this connects with the reference to the "doers of good" at the end of verse 12

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to note 14 on 31:14 for a related discussion of the pregnancy phrase.
rows.anchor: See note 14 on 31:14.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forty marks the age when a person is supposed to reach full intellectual and spiritual maturity.
rows.anchor: the age at which man is supposed to attain to full intellectual and spiritual maturity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine insan, translated 'man' or 'human being,' applies to women and men alike.
rows.anchor: the masculine noun insan ("man" or "human being") appearing in the first sentence of this verse applies to both sexes alike

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elliptical prayer means 'of whatever sin I may have committed'; Asad refers to 24:31, note 41.
rows.anchor: of whatever sin I may have cominitted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad considers this one of the earliest Medinan revelations, perhaps the earliest, and says verse 13 may date to the Prophet's hijrah.
rows.anchor: one of the earliest revelations.- perhaps the earliest - of the Medina period

rows.speaker: Ad-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr
rows.claim: They call it Meccan, but Asad rejects that view because it lacks internal and external evidence.
rows.anchor: Ad-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr (c ited by Zamakhshari) that it is a Meccan surah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title Muhammad comes from the Prophet's name in verse 2.
rows.anchor: The title is based on the mention of the name of the Prophet Muhammad in verse 2

rows.speaker: the Prophet's Companions and their immediate successors
rows.claim: Because the surah prominently treats fighting in God's cause, the Companions and early successors often called it Surat al-Qital.
rows.anchor: it was often designated by the Prophet's Companions and their immediate successors as Surat al-Qital

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this context, qawl ma'ruf means a declaration of readiness to fight in God's cause.
rows.anchor: an expression of readiness to fight in His cause: which is obviously the meaning of qawl ma'ruf in this context

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Almost all classical commentators take the rhetorical question as referring to pre-Islamic chaos, internecine wars, and moral darkness from which Islam freed its followers.
rows.anchor: almost all of the classical commentators, who regard this rhetoricaj "question" as an allusion to the chaotic conditions of pre-Islamic Arabia

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the verse and its surrounding passage also have timeless significance.
rows.anchor: this verse has, like the whole of the passage of which it forms a part, a timeless import as well
